title: Service offers for aquarium maintenance
audience: Aquarium maintenance business owners and technicians who design, price and explain service offers for client tanks
learningOutcomes: Define a service offer for aquarium maintenance with a written scope, a tier, a price basis and the exclusions
Identify recurring and add-on offers that stay within the business's scope and authority
Describe referral arrangements, and check their disclosure and fee rules before they are used
Explain honestly what the service does and does not promise to the client
referencesAtStart: Official sources for this lesson: ACCC, Small business rights and responsibilities (published and modified 7 October 2026, page metadata); business.gov.au, Australian Consumer Law and your business (27 May 2025, page metadata).

instruction.heading: What the offer is
instruction.body: A service offer is a written statement of what you will do, how often, for what price, and what the client needs to do in return. For aquarium maintenance, the core is a routine visit: testing, a planned partial water change, glass and filter care within scope, equipment checks and records. Other offers build on that core: set-up and cycle management, a trend report from the test records, an equipment check, and referrals to licensed trades. Describe every offer in the same terms, so that the client can compare them. Under the Australian Consumer Law, a service must be performed competently, suit the purpose stated, and be delivered within a reasonable time unless a timeframe was agreed (published and modified 7 October 2026 (page metadata)). Businesses owe customers honest information about services, and should keep hidden fees out of contracts (dated 27 May 2025).

instruction.heading: Three tiers that match the hobby
instruction.body: Clients differ in their experience and in how much work they want to do themselves. A basic tier covers the visit, the planned tests and the planned water change. A standard tier adds an equipment check, the records and a short monthly trend note. A full-care tier adds cycle or set-up support for a new tank and a handover pack. Use the tiers to match the client's need, not to push the most expensive one. A small study of aquarium shops in India, published in 2012 and therefore historical and not Australian, found that customers' questions centred on fish care, tank cleaning and water quality. The study's figures are not used here. It is a prompt for what to explain, and it is not evidence about the Australian market.

instruction.heading: Recurring and add-on offers
instruction.body: A recurring plan at a set interval gives the client predictable care and gives the business predictable work. Add-ons can include a test report, a filter media refresh (with materials charged under the materials cost policy), a timer or light check, and a quarantine set-up under the owner's plan. Do not sell animals, medicines or chemical treatments as add-ons. Absence care, where someone checks a tank while the owner is away, is a separate service with its own staffing, access, emergency and insurance rules.

instruction.heading: Referral partners
instruction.body: Some work is outside the business's authority and needs a licensed electrician, a licensed plumber or an animal health professional. Refer that work in writing, with the symptoms and the readings. Before you accept any payment or commission for a referral, check the rules that apply to referral fees, to advertising and to inducements in the state where you work. Disclose any arrangement to the client before they agree to the referral.

instruction.heading: Pricing for value
instruction.body: Price each offer on the work it includes: time on site, testing, records, travel, materials and the risk the work carries. Show the scope as line items, so the client can see what is included. Use the approved pricing method and quoting approval for each offer, and state the minimum charge. A receipt is needed once a transaction passes $75, and also whenever the customer asks for one (published and modified 7 October 2026 (page metadata)). Value comes from the reliability of the checks and the records, and that is what the owner is paying for.

instruction.heading: What you must not promise
instruction.body: Do not promise that the fish will live, that the water will sit at a particular value, or that a visit will fix a problem. Do not diagnose disease, and do not recommend treatments outside the owner's plan. Explain the limits of the service in writing, and keep client details private as the business policy requires.

instruction.heading: Keeping clients and growing the work
instruction.body: Clients stay with a service that is explained and recorded. A trend report, a clear handover, a reliable visit time and a plain explanation of any change are the reasons people keep a service. Ask for referrals only in ways the marketing rules allow (see the referral incentives lesson, “Referral incentives that respect consumer and spam rules”). Never send unsolicited messages to people who have not agreed to receive them.

procedure: Define the service and its scope in writing, including what is excluded.
Choose the tiers, and check each tier against the business's authority and the licence notices in this course.
Set the recurring interval and the add-ons, and confirm the materials cost policy for each one.
Price each offer under the approved pricing method and quoting approval, with a minimum charge where it applies.
Check any referral arrangement, and its disclosure and fee rules, before you offer it.
Explain the offer to the client in writing, including the limits and what is not promised.
Record the client's choice, the agreed scope and the review date.

workedExamples.situation: A client with a green-algae problem asks for a full fix and a new light, and wants one price for the whole job.
workedExamples.reasoning: Offer the standard tier, with the algae control as part of the planned care: the light period on a timer, glass cleaning, feeding and water checks. Quote the new light and any electrical work separately, and refer the electrical work to a licensed person. Explain that algae control depends on lighting, feeding and water balance, and that the offer does not promise a result. Record the client's choice.

workedExamples.situation: An electrician you know offers to pay a fee for each aquarium client you send to them. The client has not been told about it.
workedExamples.reasoning: If the arrangement goes ahead, tell each client about it before they agree to the referral, and record the disclosure. Refer on the basis of the client's need, not the fee. Do not agree to referral fees until the business has checked the disclosure rules for its state.

commonErrors.error: Offering a tier the business is not authorised to deliver.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the authority and the licence notices before the offer is made.

commonErrors.error: Quoting one price with no scope.
commonErrors.prevention: Itemise the scope and the exclusions.

commonErrors.error: Promising that the fish will live, or that a problem will be fixed.
commonErrors.prevention: Describe the service and its limits, and promise no outcome for the animals.

commonErrors.error: Taking a referral fee without disclosure.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the rules, disclose the arrangement, and refer on need.

commonErrors.error: Selling animals or treatments as add-ons.
commonErrors.prevention: Do not sell animals or treatments. Refer those requests and record them.

commonErrors.error: Offering absence care without staffing and emergency rules.
commonErrors.prevention: Set the staffing, access and emergency rules before the offer is made.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Selling, supplying or arranging the movement of live animals may need authority that this course does not grant.
Electrical and plumbing work offered through a referral is licensed work in the relevant states (see the setup and electrical lessons). This lesson does not grant any licence.
Client information is private. Share it only as the business policy allows.

qualityStandard: Every offer has a written scope, a tier, a price basis and exclusions
No offer promises an animal outcome or includes work the business is not authorised to do
Each referral arrangement is checked and disclosed before use
The client's choice and the review date are recorded
documentationEvidence: Quote or agreement with the scope and exclusions
Review date for the recurring plan
summary: A service offer is a written scope with a tier, a price basis and exclusions.
Grow the work through recurring visits, records and add-ons that stay within scope.
Check referral and commission rules, and disclose any arrangement, before you use it.
Promise the service, not an outcome for the animals.

knowledgeChecks.question: A client asks for a single price for a whole job, with no scope. What is the correct response?
options: Quote one price and do not list what is included, since the client only wants one number
Quote the lowest price the client mentions, so the job is competitive and the client is happy
Agree to the job and decide the scope later, once the work is underway on site with the client
Write an itemised scope with exclusions, and quote each part under the approved pricing method

knowledgeChecks.question: Which add-on is outside what this kind of service should offer?
options: A filter media refresh charged under the materials policy
Selling fish or chemical treatments as an add-on
A review date for the recurring plan

knowledgeChecks.question: Before you use a referral fee arrangement, what should you do?
options: Start it immediately, because referrals help the business grow faster
Hide the fee so that the client is not confused by the extra detail
Refer only clients who do not ask questions about the arrangement at all
Check the rules that apply and disclose the arrangement to the client

officialReferences.title: rules for quotes and estimates for services
officialReferences.covers: States that a customer's acceptance of a quote makes it a legally binding contract; describes a good quote as clear, specific and complete and advises writing it down; lists the work description, itemised and total costs (with GST if applicable), variations, payment terms and conditions, work start and finish dates, and a quote expiry date. Does not mention estimates or service-specific rules. Publisher: business.gov.au.
